How to Take Model Polaroids (Digitals): 6 Tips 

*Take the essential angles. Include a headshot, profile, full-length front, and full-length side or back.

* Keep your poses relaxed. Stand naturally, with a neutral expression and your hands by your sides.

* Find soft, natural light. Stand facing a window or shoot outside in open shade.

* Choose a plain background. A clean white or neutral wall keeps the focus on you.

* Wear simple, fitted clothes. Try a plain crop top with jeans, plus heels ideally for full body.

* Keep makeup and hair natural. Your features should be easy to see.

Keep the images clear, recent, and straightforward. The goal is to let you—not the styling—stand out.

3 Steps to Make your Headshots more ‘Vogue’ (Less LinkedIn 😉): 

1. Natural Light 
So natural light is what gives your skin this glow and makes it look more natural and candid even rather than clinical. When I was choosing a space for my Studio THAT was the first thing I looked for – good natural light - because it just makes everything look so much more magical and less I dunno plastic. 

So pick a Studio that has natural light. 

2. Mood Board In Depth 
Create a mood board that goes in depths into the kind of colours you’re gonna wear and the colours the background are gonna have. Keep in mind the shade of your natural skin colour, your hair, your eyes… Go into the LITTLE detail details because that’s what’s gonna give your headshot this editorial vibe. 

3. Frame your face 

Bringing your hands into the frame or have a fan for your hair to kind of also frame your face. That’s what’s gonna make the image look a lot less stiff and again more editorial … more Vogue. 🫶✨💕🙌

This is Sophie Calle’s The Shadow (1981), a project where the boundaries between watcher and watched quietly dissolve… showing us what a truly candid photo looks like.

So, Calle hired a private detective to follow her through the streets of Paris, while she simultaneously documented her own movements—turning her life into both the subject and the investigation.

What unfolds is a poetic exploration of identity, surveillance, and the fragile line between how we see ourselves and how the world observes us. The work invites us to ask a haunting question: who truly holds the gaze?
